contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Adam's descendants continued through Seth, whose line leads to Noah (Genesis 4–5).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Identify the line through Seth as a genealogical bridge, not read Genesis 4–5 as an extra episode.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Removing this contextual scene does not break an indispensable event transition already present in the nominated spine.
Genesis 6:9–22 is separately proposed as a clearly marked Scripture-source bridge establishing Noah's ark; repeating a second description of its construction immediately beforehand is unnecessary.
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Ark construction and divine command are missing before Genesis 7:1 begins with entering the Ark; source context must precede the flood.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Removing this contextual scene does not break an indispensable event transition already present in the nominated spine.
After the flood, Noah's descendants spread into peoples and nations; at Babel their language was confounded and they were scattered (Genesis 10–11).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Keep Babel as an explanatory event for dispersed nations; retain the distinction from Pentecost rather than claiming simple word-for-word symmetry.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Keep the biblical witness as a genuine cross-reference or typology when source-verified; it does not advance sequential history by itself.
Removing this contextual scene does not break an indispensable event transition already present in the nominated spine.
Isaac and Rebecca had two sons, Esau and Jacob (Genesis 25:19–26).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Name Esau and Jacob to establish the selected covenant line, not rehearse their entire youth.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Jacob received his father Isaac's blessing amid the conflict with his elder brother Esau (Genesis 27).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Indicate the paternal blessing passing to Jacob before the Bethel/Jabbok narrative.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Removing this contextual scene does not break an indispensable event transition already present in the nominated spine.
Moses was a Hebrew child rescued from Pharaoh's decree, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, and later driven into Midian (Exodus 2).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Identify who Moses is and why the cry of Israel is heard, without needing the full infancy story.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Removing this contextual scene does not break an indispensable event transition already present in the nominated spine.
Pharaoh repeatedly refused to let Israel go despite the plagues (Exodus 7–10). Moses then warned of the final judgment.
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Pharaoh's hardened resistance makes the Passover's judgment understandable without listing every plague.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Removing this contextual scene does not break an indispensable event transition already present in the nominated spine.
God guided Israel in the wilderness by a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night (Exodus 13:21–22).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Mention the cloud/fire guidance connecting departure to the crossing, without requiring every Exodus travel detail.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: In the wilderness God provided manna to sustain the people of Israel (Exodus 16).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Mention the manna as divine sustenance in the wilderness and avoid merging it with the later Bread of Life discourse.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: The Lord commanded Israel to erect the Tabernacle, where the Ark of the Covenant signified his dwelling among the people during their journey (Exodus 40:17–38).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Describe the divine dwelling in the Tabernacle, linking Sinai and Solomon's Temple without repeating architectural inventories.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Removing this contextual scene does not break an indispensable event transition already present in the nominated spine.
After the years in the wilderness, Moses commissioned Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan into the promised land (Numbers 14:33–34; Deuteronomy 31:7–8).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Name Joshua as commissioned successor before the crossing of Jordan.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Removing this contextual scene does not break an indispensable event transition already present in the nominated spine.
Ruth, a Moabite widow, remained faithful to her mother-in-law Naomi and returned with her to Bethlehem (Ruth 1:16–22).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Identify Ruth as the Moabite who remained faithful to Naomi before Ruth 4 identifies her offspring and David's lineage.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Samuel served as a prophet during Israel's transition to kingship. Saul, a Benjaminite, came to Samuel, whom the Lord had instructed to anoint him (1 Samuel 3:19–21; 9:15–27).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Identify Samuel as a prophet entrusted with guiding Israel through its transition to kingship.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Saul died in battle against the Philistines, and David subsequently began his reign over Judah at Hebron (1 Samuel 31; 2 Samuel 2:1–4).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Indicate Saul's death before David is shown receiving the kingdom.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Keep the biblical witness as a genuine cross-reference or typology when source-verified; it does not advance sequential history by itself.
David sinned grievously against Bathsheba and Uriah. Nathan confronted him, and David acknowledged his sin before the Lord (2 Samuel 11–12).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: King David's grave sin supplies a moral counterpoint to the enduring covenant, not a full additional court narrative.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: The condemnation and repentance of David are already captured in the single H34-01 context line; a second sequential retelling duplicates the same biblical development.
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Keep Nathan's condemnation and David's repentance together, without duplicating the penitential psalm as mandatory narration.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Solomon subsequently turned to foreign gods, and the Lord announced that the kingdom would be torn apart after him, though a portion would remain for David's sake (1 Kings 11:1–13).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Explain Solomon's infidelity as the direct prelude to the divided kingdom.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Elijah opposed the worship of Baal during Israel's apostasy (1 Kings 18). The following oracles of Isaiah are distinct prophetic witnesses to God's promises, not episodes occurring in one continuous scene (Isaiah 7; 9; 11; 52–53).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Use Elijah's opposition to Baal as evidence of prophetic fidelity amid idolatry; the dramatic contest is not itself mandatory reading.

After the return, Ezra publicly proclaimed the Law and the community renewed its worship of the Lord (Nehemiah 8:1–8).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Use the return of the Law and communal worship to explain restoration; Nehemiah's whole ceremony is not required.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: In later generations, foreign rulers pressured the Jewish people to forsake their law. Mattathias resisted enforced idolatry, beginning the Maccabean struggle (1 Maccabees 2:15–28).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: State the Maccabean persecution and resistance to bridge restoration and messianic expectation; do not put it in the Babylonian exile.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: The martyrs under persecution witnessed to Israel's hope in the resurrection, even in the face of death (2 Maccabees 7).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Mention witness to resurrection hope under persecution; do not require the full narrative of all seven martyrdoms.

Mary visited Elizabeth, whose child leapt at her greeting, and praised the Lord for his mercy and promises to Israel in the Magnificat (Luke 1:39–56).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Mention the Visitation/Magnificat briefly, preserving the distinct Lukan episode rather than stitching it into Matthew's Joseph account.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Matthew 1:25 explicitly states Joseph named the child Jesus; repeating the name in another editorial context note adds no new necessary narrative information. Luke 2:21 remains available in Scripture.
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Ensure the child is explicitly named Jesus, without a separate ceremonial chapter.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Mary and Joseph presented Jesus in the Temple, where Simeon recognised the promised salvation, a light to the Gentiles (Luke 2:22–32).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Simeon's recognition places the Presentation in Israel's expectation without a separate compulsory temple scene.

contextDecisions.contextPurpose: Warned that Herod threatened the child, Joseph took Jesus and Mary into Egypt. After Herod's death, the family returned and settled in Nazareth (Matthew 2:13–23).
contextDecisions.oldEditorialInstruction: Identify the return and dwelling in Nazareth as the bridge from infancy to the Forerunner.

sourceBridgeCandidates.rationale: Ark construction and Noah's response must precede the instruction to enter the ark in Genesis 7:1
From Shem's descendants to Terah/Abram before Genesis 12:1; this is a genealogical transition, not a full story

An Egyptian official purchased Joseph after his sale; following an accusation, his master imprisoned him. Genesis 39:20–21 then records God's continuing presence with Joseph. This is a short causal bridge, not a featured Potiphar episode.
sourceBridgeCandidates.oldRationale: Genesis 41 summons Joseph from imprisonment; the short bridge identifies when he entered prison without restoring his separate adventures

sourceBridgeCandidates.rationale: Existing 1 Samuel 16:10–13 opens after Samuel has already seen seven sons; the prophet's commission to Jesse must be supplied
The final miracle itself does not explain the decision to put Jesus to death; the explicit plot follows in John 11:45–53
Jesus is placed in a tomb before the next selected text begins with the empty tomb; burial is part of the death-resurrection sequence
The risen Christ appeared over forty days and instructed the apostles concerning the Spirit before Acts 1:6–12 opens mid-conversation
Acts 7:54 begins with the crowd's anger at words not yet included; the preceding accusation is essential context
Jesus promises the Spirit of Truth before Pentecost; this can replace compulsory extended farewell-discourse reading
Paul's expressed intention to see Rome supplies a short missionary-journey hinge without requiring the Philippi jailer or shipwreck
Paul actually arrives in Rome before the final proclamation pericope opens at Acts 28:23

genreAndOwnershipGuards.notes: Isaiah's pronouncements, Matthew and Luke genealogies, apostolic letters and Revelation visions cannot be presented as dated events within one eyewitness timeline.
Luke's Last Supper, John's farewell discourse, Matthew's trial and John's scourging must have distinct original citation labels and no composed composite 'Bible quote'.
No reintroduction of detailed Judges, Daniel/Tobit/Judith/Esther, Philippi prison or Acts shipwreck is authorized merely because a one-verse bridge is needed.
Source references remain with existing 73-book Catholic Scripture witnesses; no new parallel or extended experience is proposed.
